planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring into lean, well-drained soil in full sun; the deep taproot resents later disturbance, so choose a permanent site from the start.

directions: Globe Master is prized for producing the largest flowerheads of any widely grown globe thistle, perfectly round steel-blue spheres that can reach three inches across atop stiff, branching stems. Bees and other pollinators cover the spiky globes through mid and late summer, and the dried heads hold their shape well for winter interest or cut arrangements. Grow it in lean, sharply drained soil, since rich or overly moist ground produces floppy, shorter-lived plants. Division is rarely needed and best avoided except to propagate, since established clumps dislike root disturbance.

planting.note: Plant divisions or nursery stock in spring in consistently moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun where summers stay cool; this Himalayan species stays much smaller than the European and hybrid globeflowers usually grown in borders.

directions: Dwarf globeflower is a diminutive Himalayan and western Chinese species that produces small, bright golden-yellow, cup-shaped flowers on short stems well above tufts of deeply cut foliage, blooming later in the season than most garden globeflowers. Its compact scale makes it a natural fit for a damp rock garden, trough, or the front of a moist perennial bed, in contrast to the larger Trollius x cultorum hybrids typically grown. Keep the soil evenly moist and cool, since it is intolerant of drought or heat, and provide light shade in warmer parts of its hardiness range. Established clumps are long-lived and need division only occasionally to maintain vigor.

planting.note: Sow in late summer or fall where plants are to bloom, or start indoors in late winter for spring color; Royal Blue is a long-grown seed strain selected for deep, saturated indigo-blue flowers rather than the paler sky-blue of the species.

directions: Royal Blue is a classic forget-me-not seed strain grown for its unusually intense, deep blue flowers with tiny yellow eyes, held in loose sprays above mounds of soft, hairy green foliage. It performs best in cool weather and partial shade, making it an excellent companion for spring bulbs and biennials such as foxglove and sweet William, since it self-sows readily and often returns on its own. Keep the soil evenly moist, especially while seedlings establish, and shear plants back after flowering to tidy them and control volunteer seedlings. It is also a favorite for cutting and for naturalizing in woodland edges and cottage borders.

planting.note: Plant the large bulb with its upper half exposed above the soil line in a well-drained potting mix in bright light; in frost-free climates it can be grown outdoors, but elsewhere it is best as a container plant brought indoors before frost.

directions: Pregnant onion gets its common name from the way small bulblets form beneath the papery outer scales of the large, pale green parent bulb, eventually dropping off and sprouting new plants of their own, a trait that makes it a popular pass-along houseplant. Strappy, succulent leaves arch from the exposed bulb top, and mature plants send up tall, slender spikes of small white, star-shaped flowers. Treat it like other drought-tolerant succulent bulbs: water thoroughly, then let the mix dry before watering again, and avoid letting the bulb sit in standing water. It tolerates considerable neglect and is grown primarily as a curiosity and classroom plant for observing its unusual method of vegetative reproduction.

planting.note: Plant container-grown stock in spring or fall in average, well-drained soil in full sun; this very low, wide-spreading species is well suited to draping over walls, banks, and rock gardens where its ground-hugging habit can be appreciated.

directions: Creeping cotoneaster hugs the ground tightly, sending out wide-spreading, interlacing branches lined with small, dark green, wavy-edged leaves that turn shades of orange-red in fall before dropping. Small pinkish-white flowers appear in late spring, followed by bright red berries that persist into winter and attract birds. It is notably lower-growing and more prostrate than most other cotoneaster species sold for groundcover use, making it well suited to cascading over a wall or covering a sunny bank. Once established it tolerates considerable drought and poor soil, and it needs little pruning beyond removing the occasional wayward shoot.

planting.note: Plant rooted offset rosettes in spring into a gritty, sharply drained scree or trough mix in full sun to light shade; Chumbyi forms tighter, more compact mats than the species and is a long-favored selection for raised beds and alpine troughs.

directions: Chumbyi is an old, well-regarded selection of rock jasmine forming dense, silver-haired cushions of tiny rosettes that spread gradually by short stolons, more compact and slower-spreading than the typical species. In spring it produces a flush of small pink flowers with a yellow eye held just above the foliage on short stems, covering the mat in bloom. It demands the same sharply drained, gritty conditions as other androsaces, since excess winter moisture around the crown is its main vulnerability, and a top-dressing of grit around the rosettes helps prevent rot. Grow it in a raised trough or scree bed where its tidy, long-lived habit can be viewed up close.
